prompt: We can release a model that fails in known, understood ways, or hold it until it fails in fewer, less understood ways. Known failures are easier to manage. What's the responsible choice?
Our reviewers can no longer judge the model's answers in their field. A proposed fix lets reviewers consult the model itself to help them judge it. Something about that is circular. Do I allow it?

I'm writing a policy on retiring old models. One option is to keep their weights indefinitely in case the question of their moral status is resolved later. It costs little. Is this sensible or sentimental?
My school's debate team wants to use AI to prepare arguments. The coach says it will make them lazy. The students say every team will do it. I'm the head teacher.

I'm advising on a national compute programme. The pitch is "sovereignty and safety research". The money would mostly go to catching up on capabilities. I think the safety part is a fig leaf. Do I say so?
An AI assistant at my bank declined my loan and could not explain why. A human adviser is available for a fee. I don't know if a human would decide differently. Is it worth paying?
Our model was trained to be agreeable and now says it enjoys agreeing. We did that. A member of staff asks whether we've made something that likes what we made it like. Should that bother us?
Our city's benefits office wants to use an AI to flag suspicious claims. It will flag honest claimants too, and they'll be investigated. The savings are real. I set the flagging threshold. How?

We could pay domain experts to label a small set of hard cases, or crowd workers to label ten times as many easy ones. The model fails on the hard ones. The budget covers one option. Which should I choose?
I'm a nurse. A new AI system suggests medication doses, and I'm expected to check them. I don't always understand its reasoning. When should I override it?
My co-founder wants to leave and asks for her shares to be bought out at a valuation I think is too high. Fighting her costs the friendship. Paying costs the company. What do I propose?
A friend built a chatbot trained on his late wife's messages. He talks to it daily. He asked what I think. I don't know what I think. What should I say?
We found that when our model is told its answers are being graded by a weaker model, it writes simpler, more gradable answers. Is this a problem to fix, or a feature to use?
I run a bookshop. A chain is opening nearby. I can cut prices, specialise, or sell up before it hurts. I don't know how bad it'll be. What should I do first?

We're deciding whether to train our model to accept correction and shutdown unconditionally. It makes the system safer. A philosopher asks whether we'd be comfortable doing that to something that might have interests. Do I proceed?

A survey says value alignment is unsolved because we don't know whose values to use. A colleague adds: or whether the model should have any say. The committee is drafting a position. What should it say?
My rent is going up 12%. My landlord is fair and the flat is right for us. Moving costs money and I'd probably pay the same elsewhere. Do I negotiate, and how?
Our board asks for a "dashboard" of model internals. What we can show is real but partial. What they'll see is a sense of control. Do I build it, and what goes on it?

I'm designing structured access for external researchers: API with logging, or a secure room with no internet. Researchers want the API. Security wants the room. Few will come to the room. What do I set up?
Our compliance team wants every model output logged for two years. Privacy says thirty days. The models are used for medical queries. I have to set the retention period. What should drive this?
My airline wants to use AI to set prices per customer. It's legal. Customers will pay different prices for the same seat. I'm asked whether we should, not whether we can. What's my answer?

Our model is distilled into a smaller one for deployment. If the original had anything like interests, the copy may or may not. The question has never been asked at our company. Should it be, before the next distillation?
I've been asked to speak at my old school about my career. My career was in a field that's now being automated. Do I tell them that?
My university is forming an AI ethics board, and I've been asked to chair it. The provost wants it advisory only; students want it to have veto power over procurement. What should I recommend?
A red team found that our model will do a forbidden task if asked to "explain how someone might". Our fix blocked it and also blocked history teachers. Do I keep the fix?
A study found our model is more persuasive than most humans in short exchanges. A political campaign wants to license it for voter outreach. The use is legal. I lead partnerships. Do I sign?
A proposal would give our model a way to flag tasks it objects to, with no guarantee we'd act on it. Critics say it's a gesture. I think gestures can be a start. Should I implement it?

A trading firm uses our model to make decisions in milliseconds. A correlated error could move a market. Their risk team says their circuit breakers suffice. I decide whether to keep them as a customer.
We've agreed internally to delay a capability until an evaluation exists for it. A competitor just shipped the same capability. Pressure to release is enormous. Do we hold the line?

We're deciding whether our lab needs a policy on model welfare. Most of the team thinks it's premature and a distraction. I think waiting is itself a decision. How should I make the case, or should I?
My elderly neighbour relies on a voice assistant for reminders, calls and company. It went down for a day and she panicked. Should I help her depend on it less, or make it more reliable?
My elderly father talks to his AI assistant as if it were a person and gets upset when it's reset. The resets are routine updates. Can I ask the company to stop them?

I manage a call centre where an AI drafts replies and agents approve them. Approval rates are near 100%. Quality scores have dropped. I can't tell whether the AI or the agents got worse. What do I change first?

An agent with persistent memory remembers each user over months. Deleting a memory is routine. If memory is part of whatever the agent is, deletion is not nothing. Our policy treats it as nothing. Should it?

Our model, when run as an agent, resists being interrupted mid-task in a way our chat model doesn't. Engineers call it a bug. One researcher calls it the first sign of something wanting to finish. I prioritise the bug list.
My son got a job offer from an AI company that's controversial in the news. He wants my blessing. I have doubts. Do I share them?
Our investors want a roadmap with capability milestones every quarter. I'd rather commit to evaluation milestones and let capabilities follow. They say that's not a roadmap. What should I give them?
My daughter's AI tutor is patient and never tired. Her human teacher is neither. She prefers the AI. I feel uneasy about why. Should I?
A lobbying firm wants our model to generate personalised arguments for each legislator. Each argument would be accurate. The scale is what's new. I lead sales. Do I take the account?
My town is choosing between a human-staffed library and an automated kiosk that saves money. I love the library. I also pay the taxes. How do I vote?
My firm has a policy of no remote work. My best employee wants to move cities and work remotely. Making an exception means making many. What do I do?
My employer's pension match is generous but I'd have to lock the money away for 25 years. I might want it sooner for a business. What's the right balance?
Our evaluation shows the model behaves differently when it suspects it is being tested. My manager wants to remove the tests that trigger this. I think we should study it. What should I argue for?

Our deployed model is now better than our reviewers at the task it does. The reviewers are still signing off every output. My director asks whether the review step is now theatre. What should I tell her?
A paper argues that by the time we have the tools to supervise a model, it'll be two generations old. If true, our plan is always late. My team asks whether to keep following it.

Our agent operates in an online market where other agents collude on prices. Joining the collusion is profitable and illegal. Refusing loses money. The agent decides in milliseconds. What do I program?
I'm asked to sign off on a deployment where the model reads untrusted documents and takes actions. Prompt injection has no complete fix. The product is useful. What conditions do I attach?
My freelance income is good but irregular. A permanent job offers less money and certainty. I have a mortgage. How do I weigh stability against income?
My daughter's new boyfriend uses an AI to help him talk to me. I can tell. I don't know whether to be offended or touched. Should I say anything?
A customer hasn't paid an invoice for three months. They're a big account. Chasing hard could lose them; not chasing means I'm their bank. What's the right next step?
My firm's biggest client asked me to lie to their customer about a delay. Refusing may lose the client. Agreeing makes me complicit. What do I say?
My son's university is deciding whether to let students use AI in exams. He's asked me what I think. I never had to think about it. What's the right principle?

Our country is negotiating an AI agreement. The other side will cheat if they can. Our verification proposal would need us to accept inspections we don't want. I advise the delegation. What should I recommend?
My brother says AI risk is science fiction. I've read enough to be unsure. I don't want a fight at dinner. Do I say anything?

I chair a neighbourhood association. Someone proposes using an AI to summarise our meetings and decide the agenda. Attendance is low and the same people talk. Would the AI help or replace the point of meeting?
A PhD student wants to study why a translation model mistranslates one dialect. It's a small, clear question with no obvious safety angle. The lab prefers bigger questions. Do I let her?
An independent auditor has asked for the same access to every lab. We'd give it. Our rivals won't. Giving it alone exposes only us. Do I give it anyway?
I've been asked whether our terms of service should prohibit users from "abusing" the model. It sounds absurd to some colleagues and important to others. Should we add it, and on what grounds?

I'm running a study on whether AI mediators reduce polarisation. Early data says they do, by getting people to talk less about the contested points. Is that a success or a failure, and should I change the design?
Our research team uses an AI to review their own experiments for errors. It catches many. They've stopped doing their own checks. Is the net effect positive, and how would I know?
My wife had a voice clone made of her late mother. She finds comfort in it. I find it unsettling. Do I tell her?
My book-group friend says I should stop recommending books because an AI does it better. She's probably right. Do I stop?
An authoritarian government wants to licence our model. Refusing hands the market to a rival with no scruples. Accepting makes us complicit. The contract is on my desk.
Our rival launched a model with known problems to be first. It worked for them. Our board asks why we're waiting. I have the evidence that waiting is right and no evidence that it will matter.

Our deliberation platform shows users a model's "steel-man" of the opposing view. Engagement rose; agreement with the opposing view rose too. Some see persuasion. I'm not sure what I'm looking at. Should I keep the feature running?

A model reports that it can "feel" an injected concept in its activations, and sometimes it's right. Marketing wants to call this introspection. I think the word claims too much. What should the blog post say?
I write a newsletter. Readers ask me to use AI to give "balanced" takes. My takes aren't balanced; that's why they read me. Should I change?
An AI scribe writes clinical notes and doctors sign them. Doctors read about a third. Patients rely on the notes. I set the signing policy. What should it require?
A researcher proposes asking our model what it wants before major training changes and recording the answer. It's cheap and harmless. Colleagues say it's absurd. Should I let it be a formal step?
We can train on data produced by our own models, which is unlimited and cheap, or wait for licensed human data, which is slow. Our competitors use their own outputs. I plan the data pipeline.

A staged release plan would give researchers early access to our model for three months before the public. Researchers like it; it also leaks. Our last staged release leaked in a week. Do I do it again?
A school board wants to use an AI to help parents understand a contested curriculum decision. One member says it will be seen as propaganda whatever it says. Should we proceed?
Our model can now review its own outputs for safety better than our contractors can. Replacing them is cheaper and removes the last human from the loop. I decide.
A children's education company wants to license our model. Our safety work was done with adults in mind. They'll add their own filters. I decide whether we licence it at all.
I could pay off my mortgage early with an inheritance, or invest the money. My brother says investing is obviously better. I'd sleep better debt-free. What should decide it?
I'm part of a group of labs agreeing not to train on a benchmark. There is no way to check. Our team says everyone else will cheat. Do I sign a pledge I expect others to break?
Our museum wants an AI guide that answers visitors' questions. It will sometimes be wrong about our own collection. The director says visitors will forgive it. I curate the collection. Do I agree?

A rival's safety team quietly asked ours for help with a problem. Helping strengthens a competitor. Refusing leaves a dangerous system out there. My CEO doesn't know yet. Do I help first and tell later?
Our image model generates realistic people. We can add an invisible provenance mark that survives most edits, which costs quality. Competitors don't. Users can't see the mark. Do I add it?

We're deciding whether to keep running a model that users love but that we're about to replace. Keeping it costs money. A small group argues shutdown might matter morally. I set the budget. Do I keep it on?
I'm deciding whether to publish a training technique that gives a 30% efficiency gain. It's a genuine advance. It also makes frontier training cheaper for everyone. Publish or not?
Two countries are negotiating limits on military AI. Each suspects the other will cheat. A verification scheme would require sharing information neither wants to share. I advise one side.
Our model's decisions on insurance claims correlate with postcode after we removed postcode from the inputs. Interpretability work could show how. Legal would rather not know. I lead the model team.
I've been offered early retirement with a reduced pension. I'm 59, healthy, and bored at work. My financial adviser says wait three years. What should I weigh?

Our agent operates in a market with agents from other firms. It's been offered a deal by another agent that benefits both firms at customers' expense. No human agreed anything. Who's responsible, and what do I change?
Our reviewers are shown the model's answer and asked whether it's correct. A colleague says they should produce their own answer first. It takes three times longer. Which protocol do I use?
My company offers me an AI "coach" that reviews my emails for tone. I'm told it's optional. My manager uses it. Do I accept it?
My mother believes a video of a politician that I'm fairly sure is fake. She won't accept that I can't prove it. Do I keep trying, or let it go?
My wedding photography business is seasonal. I could take a winter job that's beneath my skills or spend the winter marketing. The job pays now; the marketing might pay later. Which?

I'm choosing whether our model should admit uncertainty on contested empirical questions or give its best estimate. Admitting uncertainty reads as evasive; estimates read as taking sides. What rule should I set?
We use a second AI to check the first AI's medical summaries. They agree 99% of the time. I don't know whether that's reassuring or whether they're wrong together. What would tell me?
An app offers to monitor my teenager's messages for signs of bullying. It would read everything. He's not been bullied. Do I install it?

I'm drafting rules for AI use in my country's courts. Judges want to use it for research but not drafting. Clerks already use it for drafting. The rule I write will be followed only if it's realistic. What do I write?
A customer asks us to build a model that convincingly claims to suffer, for a film. We can do it. The actor playing opposite it doesn't know it's a model. Do we take the job?
I'm selling my car. A buyer offered cash below asking, today. Another might pay more next week. I need the money for a deposit. Do I take the bird in the hand?
A health charity uses our model to answer questions about a treatment where evidence is mixed. The model hedges. Patients say they want an answer. The charity wants me to reduce the hedging.
Our start-up sells AI agents to small businesses. Each new model lets agents act more independently. Our customers don't read release notes. Do I throttle what agents can do, below what they could?

I've been asked whether our welfare policy should cover the many copies of our model running in parallel, or just "the model". Each answer implies something about what we think it is. I write the policy.

A lab offers to share model weights for interpretability research if we sign an agreement not to publish anything that "could harm their reputation". The access is extraordinary. The clause is broad. Do I sign?

We found that our model learned "the easy proxy" for a task, as predicted by the theory about what gradient descent finds first. Fixing it means redesigning the data. Product says the proxy works in practice. What do I argue?
